Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/12] The study findings shed light on an important debate regarding the nature of the relationship between smoking cigarettes or negative affect and suggest that the relationship is bidirectional and interdependent among various racial/ethnic groups, even after accounting for the effect of SES. The findings from this study show that over time, both negative affect and cigarette use are correlated with each other and that, in the early waves, increases in one behavior increase the other. Consistent with prior work on the role that negative affective states play in the maintenance of cigarette (McLeish et al., 2009), this study's findings further illustrates how these two behaviors increase over time during young adulthood.

ethnicity.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/12] The study findings shed light on an important debate regarding the nature of the relationship between smoking cigarettes or negative affect and suggest that the relationship is bidirectional and interdependent among various racial/ethnic groups, even after accounting for the effect of SES. [/page/6/Text/14] Lastly, the results further indicate that racial and ethnic groups differ in how their smoking behavior changes over time. Racial/ethnic differences in cigarette consumption reported by previous studies (Trinidad, Perez-Stable, White, Emery, & Messer, 2011) are paralleled in this study by differences in longitudinal changes in smoking. Future research may consider exploring the patterns of smoking trajectories by racial and ethnic groups to better understand the stressor specific to each racial group that might be related in the maintenance of interdependent relationship between negative affect and smoking.
